lessons.title: Coordinates on a grid
lessons.summary: Read and plot signed coordinates in the four quadrants and on the axes.
lessons.objective: Read and plot signed coordinates in the four quadrants and on the axes.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
Read coordinates in the order horizontal, then vertical.

Read each signed distance from its own axis.

On the vertical axis the x-coordinate is zero. On the horizontal axis the y-coordinate is zero.
lessons.method:
Which coordinate should I read first?

Start at the vertical axis and count horizontal units. Then measure the vertical position from the horizontal axis.

How can I decide the signs?

Right and up are positive. Left and down are negative. Start counting both directions from the origin.

How do I describe a point on an axis?

On the y-axis there is no horizontal change. On the x-axis there is no vertical change.
mistakes: The label beside a point belongs to the dot. Read the dot rather than the text label.
The two coordinates can have different signs.
Keep the zero in the correct position in the ordered pair.

examples.title: Read the coordinates of a marked point
examples.question: Write down the coordinates of P on the grid.
examples.solution:
Read the horizontal value first.

The point is at x = \(-1\) and y = \(-4\).

The coordinates are \((-1,-4)\).

examples.title: Translate movements from the origin into coordinates
examples.question: Start at the origin, move 1 units right and 8 units down. State the new coordinates.
examples.solution:
Read the horizontal move as the x-coordinate.

A downward move from the origin gives a negative y-coordinate.

The coordinates are \((1,-8)\).

examples.title: Place a point on a named axis
examples.question: Q lies on the y-axis and has a y-coordinate of 1. Give its coordinates.
examples.solution:
Every point on the vertical axis has x-coordinate zero.

Keep the stated y-coordinate \(1\).

The coordinates are \((0,1)\).

lessons.title: Drawing straight-line graphs
lessons.summary: Use an equation or a table of values to plot and draw a straight line.
lessons.objective: Use an equation or a table of values to plot and draw a straight line.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
Two points fix a straight line. Use a third location as a check.

Find the missing coordinate by substituting the known one.

A line with constant y is horizontal.
lessons.method:
How do I build the table?

Pick horizontal values and substitute each into the equation. Record the matching vertical results in the same row.

What does it mean that a point lies on a line?

A point belongs on the line if its two coordinates make the equation true.

How can I draw a line with constant y?

All points share the same vertical position. Their horizontal coordinates can change.
mistakes: The two axes can use different units. Label their scales before plotting.
Preserve the order of the coordinates when writing the point.
The equation of a vertical line keeps x constant instead.

examples.title: Complete a table value before drawing a line
examples.question: Find the y-value for x = 5 on the graph of \(y=-5x+6\).
examples.solution:
Replace x by \(5\) in the rule.

Evaluate \(-5\times5+6\).

The answer is \(-19\).

examples.title: Find a point that belongs to the line
examples.question: On \(y=6x+7\), give the point with x-coordinate 6.
examples.solution:
Use the given x-coordinate to find y from the line's equation.

Write the two coordinates in the order (x, y).

The coordinates are \((6,43)\).

examples.title: Read a horizontal line
examples.question: For the line \(y=8\), find the y-coordinate at x = 7.
examples.solution:
The equation gives the same y for every horizontal position.

A horizontal line holds its y-coordinate constant.

The answer is \(8\).

lessons.title: Finding gradient from a grid
lessons.summary: Use a right-angled change triangle to find positive and negative gradients from a grid.
lessons.objective: Use a right-angled change triangle to find positive and negative gradients from a grid.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
Divide the signed vertical change by the horizontal change.

Use the negative sign when the vertical value falls.

Choose grid crossings spaced well apart to make the changes easy to read.
lessons.method:
Which way should I measure the changes?

Pick two points on the line. Move from the left point to the right point to give a positive horizontal run.

How do I mark a falling line's gradient?

Moving left to right on a falling line gives a negative vertical change.

Does the triangle have to start at the origin?

On a straight line every pair of points gives the same ratio of vertical to horizontal change.
mistakes: The grid scale tells you how many units each square represents.
A gradient measures steepness and direction.
A height on the vertical axis is different from a change in height.

examples.title: Use the change in y over the change in x
examples.question: Find the exact gradient of the line through A and B on the grid.
examples.solution:
Moving from A to B changes x by \(6\) and y by \(5\).

Divide the vertical change by the horizontal change: \(\frac{5}{6}\).

The answer is \(\frac{5}{6}\).

examples.title: Use the change in y over the change in x
examples.question: Find the exact gradient of the line through A and B on the grid.
examples.solution:
Moving from A to B changes x by \(6\) and y by \(-6\).

Divide the vertical change by the horizontal change: \(-1\).

The answer is \(-1\).

examples.title: Use the change in y over the change in x
examples.question: Find the exact gradient of the line through A and B on the grid.
examples.solution:
Moving from A to B changes x by \(6\) and y by \(7\).

Divide the vertical change by the horizontal change: \(\frac{7}{6}\).

The answer is \(\frac{7}{6}\).

lessons.title: Finding gradient from coordinates (Extended)
lessons.summary: Use differences between two given points to calculate a gradient without drawing the line.
lessons.objective: Use differences between two given points to calculate a gradient without drawing the line.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
Gradient is \(\frac{y_2-y_1}{x_2-x_1}\) when the x-coordinates differ.

Check the sign against the movement from the left point to the right point.

Horizontal lines have gradient zero. Vertical lines have an undefined gradient.
lessons.method:
Which differences form the fraction?

Subtract the starting x from the ending x. In the same order subtract the starting y from the ending y.

Can I check against a sketch?

Look at the two points. If y decreases while x increases, the gradient is negative.

How do I reason about a vertical line?

Equal x-coordinates give no horizontal change, so the gradient fraction has a zero denominator.
mistakes: Subtract both differences in the same order.
Reverse both subtractions together if you change the order.
An undefined gradient is not zero.

examples.title: Use the change in y over the change in x
examples.question: Find the exact gradient of the line through \((-6, 1)\) and \((4, -5)\).
examples.solution:
Moving from A to B changes x by \(10\) and y by \(-6\).

Divide the vertical change by the horizontal change: \(-\frac{3}{5}\).

The answer is \(-\frac{3}{5}\).

examples.title: Use the change in y over the change in x
examples.question: Find the exact gradient of the line through \((-7, -1)\) and \((5, 6)\).
examples.solution:
Moving from A to B changes x by \(12\) and y by \(7\).

Divide the vertical change by the horizontal change: \(\frac{7}{12}\).

The answer is \(\frac{7}{12}\).

examples.title: Identify the gradient of an axis-aligned line
examples.question: Is the gradient of the line through \((1, -7)\) and \((1, 3)\) zero or undefined?
examples.solution:
The x-coordinates match, giving no horizontal change.

A zero vertical change gives zero gradient; a zero horizontal change makes the gradient undefined.

lessons.title: Midpoint and length of a segment (Extended)
lessons.summary: Average matched coordinates for midpoint and use a right triangle for length.
lessons.objective: Average matched coordinates for midpoint and use a right triangle for length.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
Take the mean of the two x-values and the mean of the two y-values.

Square the two lengths, add the squares and take the positive square root.

Double the midpoint, then subtract the matching coordinate of the known endpoint.
lessons.method:
Which coordinates do I average?

The midpoint is halfway across both horizontally and vertically. The two coordinate averages separate these steps.

How can I find the straight-line distance?

The horizontal and vertical changes make the legs of a right triangle. The segment is the hypotenuse.

Can the midpoint give me a missing endpoint?

The displacement from the first endpoint to the midpoint repeats from the midpoint to the far endpoint.
mistakes: Do not average all four coordinates together.
Take absolute changes for lengths. Their squares remove the signs anyway.
Use separate x and y calculations.

examples.title: Find the midpoint of a segment
examples.question: Find the midpoint of the segment from \((-5,6)\) to \((1,1)\).
examples.solution:
Take the mean of the two x-coordinates and the mean of the two y-coordinates.

The means are \(-2\) and \(\frac{7}{2}\).

The coordinates are \((-2,\frac{7}{2})\).

examples.title: Find the exact length using a coordinate triangle
examples.question: Find the exact length of the segment from \((-6,7)\) to \((1,1)\).
examples.solution:
The horizontal and vertical changes have lengths 7 and 6.

Pythagoras gives squared length \(7^2+6^2=85\).

The length is \(\sqrt{85}\).

examples.title: Find the missing endpoint from the midpoint
examples.question: One endpoint of a segment is \((-7,8)\) and its midpoint is \((-3,\frac{9}{2})\). Give the other endpoint.
examples.solution:
The step from the first endpoint to the midpoint is the same as the step from the midpoint to the second endpoint.

Double each midpoint coordinate, then subtract the corresponding given endpoint coordinate.

The coordinates are \((1,1)\).

lessons.title: Finding equations of straight lines
lessons.summary: Use the given gradient and intercept or a known point to write a line equation.
lessons.objective: Use the given gradient and intercept or a known point to write a line equation.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
In \(y=mx+c\), \(m\) is the gradient and \(c\) is the y-intercept.

Substitute both coordinates and solve for the intercept.

Use the gradient and vertical intercept read from the grid.

Read the point where the line meets the horizontal axis and set x equal to that value.
lessons.method:
What do m and c represent?

A non-vertical line can be written with y as the subject. Its x coefficient gives slope and the constant gives the vertical-axis crossing.

How does one point locate a line with known gradient?

Use the known gradient and write a placeholder for the intercept. The coordinates of the point make this equation true.

How can I read a line equation from a grid?

Mark the intercept and find a second point on the line. Read the rise per unit run.

What is the equation of a vertical line?

Every point on the line uses the same horizontal coordinate. This line is specified by x alone.
mistakes: The y-intercept is a position. The gradient describes a change.
A point off the vertical axis does not directly give the intercept.
A horizontal-axis crossing is different from the y-intercept.
A vertical line keeps x constant. A horizontal line keeps y constant.

examples.title: Find a line from its gradient and intercept
examples.question: Write the equation of the line with gradient \(-5\) and y-intercept \(6\).
examples.solution:
Use the form y = mx + c.

The gradient gives the coefficient of x. The y-intercept gives the constant \(6\).

The equation is \(y=-5x+6\).

examples.title: Use a gradient and a point
examples.question: Find the equation of the line with gradient \(6\) through \((-6,-29)\).
examples.solution:
Use the given gradient. The unknown intercept c is the remaining number.

Put the point into the equation: \(-29=6\times(-6)+c\). Solve for c.

The equation is \(y=6x+7\).

examples.title: Read the gradient and intercept from a grid
examples.question: Write the equation of the straight line on the grid.
examples.solution:
The line crosses the y-axis at \(2\).

From A to B, x increases by one and the change in y is \(-1\).

The equation is \(y=-x+2\).

examples.title: Read the equation of a vertical line
examples.question: Write the equation of the vertical line on the grid.
examples.solution:
A vertical line has the same x-coordinate everywhere.

It meets the x-axis at \(2\), so that x-coordinate is constant.

The equation is \(x=2\).

lessons.title: Parallel lines
lessons.summary: Identify the same gradient and use the requested intercept or point to write a different line.
lessons.objective: Identify the same gradient and use the requested intercept or point to write a different line.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
Use the same gradient for a non-vertical parallel line.

Write a new equation using the old slope and the given intercept.

Solve for the new intercept after substituting the point.
lessons.method:
Which part of a line stays the same?

Parallel lines have the same direction. The vertical change per horizontal unit stays the same.

How do I use a new intercept?

Keep the gradient you already found. Use the new intercept for the constant term.

How can a known point fix the parallel line?

A different point may require a different intercept. Substitute the point with the same gradient.
mistakes: Two equations with the same gradient and intercept describe one line.
Compare the intercepts to check that the lines are distinct.
Do not keep the old intercept unless the point lies on the old line.

examples.title: Use the gradient of a parallel line
examples.question: A line is parallel to \(y=-5x+6\). What is its gradient?
examples.solution:
The given line has gradient \(-5\).

A parallel line has the same gradient.

The answer is \(-5\).

examples.title: Write a parallel line with a given intercept
examples.question: Find the equation of the line parallel to \(y=6x-7\) with y-intercept \(9\).
examples.solution:
Parallel lines have the same gradient.

Keep the coefficient of x, then use the new y-intercept \(9\).

The equation is \(y=6x+9\).

examples.title: Write a parallel line through a given point
examples.question: Find the equation of the line parallel to \(y=-7x-8\) which passes through \((-7,59)\).
examples.solution:
Keep the same gradient and write an unknown constant.

Substitute the coordinates \((-7,59)\) and solve for the constant.

The equation is \(y=-7x+10\).

lessons.title: Perpendicular lines (Extended)
lessons.summary: Find a perpendicular gradient and handle vertical and horizontal cases.
lessons.objective: Find a perpendicular gradient and handle vertical and horizontal cases.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
Multiply the two gradients to get \(-1\).

Solve for the new intercept using the point and its perpendicular gradient.

A horizontal line has a constant y-coordinate. A vertical line has a constant x-coordinate.
lessons.method:
What happens to the gradient at a right angle?

If both lines have non-zero finite gradients, turn the change triangle by a quarter turn. Its rise and run swap roles and change sign.

How do I locate the perpendicular through a point?

First calculate the new gradient. Then use the point given for the new line, which need not lie on the original.

What if one line is horizontal or vertical?

A horizontal line and a vertical line meet at a right angle. A reciprocal calculation is unnecessary in this case.
mistakes: Changing the sign alone works only when the first gradient has magnitude one.
The point is on the new line. Use it with the new gradient.
Do not divide by zero when finding a perpendicular to a horizontal line.

examples.title: Find the negative reciprocal gradient
examples.question: Find the gradient of a line perpendicular to \(y=-x+9\). Give the exact value.
examples.solution:
The stated gradient is \(-1\).

Its negative reciprocal makes the product equal to \(-1\).

The answer is \(1\).

examples.title: Write the perpendicular line through a point
examples.question: Find the equation of the line perpendicular to \(y=x+10\) which passes through \((7,-1)\).
examples.solution:
The new gradient is the negative reciprocal, \(-1\).

Use the known point to locate the intercept. Substitute x and y into the new line equation.

The equation is \(y=-x+6\).

examples.title: Handle horizontal and vertical perpendicular lines
examples.question: A line perpendicular to \(y=11\) passes through \((6,-7)\). Give its equation.
examples.solution:
The given line is horizontal. Its perpendicular is vertical.

All points on the new line have x-coordinate \(6\).

The equation is \(x=6\).

lessons.title: Straight lines in general form (Extended)
lessons.summary: Rearrange a line equation, identify its gradient and draw it from its intercepts.
lessons.objective: Rearrange a line equation, identify its gradient and draw it from its intercepts.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
In \(Ax+By=C\), divide by \(B\) to get \(y=-\frac{A}{B}x+\frac{C}{B}\) when \(B\ne 0\).

Set y equal to zero for the x-intercept. Set x equal to zero for the y-intercept.

Moving from \(y=mx+c\) to \(Ax+By=C\) leaves the same set of points.
lessons.method:
How do I find the gradient when y is not alone?

Move the x-term across the equals sign. Then divide every term by the coefficient of y.

How can I draw the line from its intercepts?

At each crossing, one coordinate is zero. Find both intercepts, place them on labelled axes and join them.

How do I clear the denominator when rewriting a line?

Choose a common multiple of the denominators. Multiply each term by it, then collect the variables on the left.
mistakes: The negative sign appears because the x-term changes side.
If both crossings are the origin, use a different point to draw the line.
Use the same multiplier for every term and for both sides.

examples.title: Read the gradient from a general-form line
examples.question: Find the gradient of \(5x+6y=42\).
examples.solution:
Move the x-term to the right, then divide every term by the coefficient of y.

In \(y=-\frac{5}{6}x+7\), the coefficient of x is the gradient.

The answer is \(-\frac{5}{6}\).

examples.title: Find where a standard-form line meets the axes
examples.question: Find the x-coordinate where \(6x+7y=56\) crosses the x-axis.
examples.solution:
At the x-axis, y is zero. At the y-axis, x is zero.

Substitute zero for y and solve \(6x=56\).

At the y-axis the crossing is \((0,8)\). Plot both points and draw the line.

The answer is \(\frac{28}{3}\).

examples.title: Rewrite a line in general form
examples.question: Give an equivalent equation to \(y=-\frac{1}{4}x+9\). You can clear the denominator to write it in general form.
examples.solution:
Multiply the entire equation by \(8\) to remove the denominator.

This gives \(8y=-2x+72\). Move the x-term to the left and simplify common factors if desired.

The equation is \(2x+8y=72\).

lessons.title: Equations of perpendicular bisectors (Extended)
lessons.summary: Find a line that passes through the midpoint of a segment and meets it at a right angle.
lessons.objective: Find a line that passes through the midpoint of a segment and meets it at a right angle.
lessons.before: Read the two coordinate scales from the origin.
lessons.ideas:
Average the x-coordinates and the y-coordinates to get the midpoint.

For a non-zero finite gradient \(m\), the bisector gradient is \(-\frac1m\). Substitute the midpoint to find the intercept.

If the segment is horizontal, use the x-coordinate of the midpoint. If it is vertical, use the midpoint's y-coordinate for a horizontal bisector.
lessons.method:
Which point must the bisector pass through?

A perpendicular bisector cuts one segment into two equal lengths. The cut is therefore at the midpoint.

How do I find the new line's gradient?

First find the gradient of the segment. To turn the direction through a right angle, use its negative reciprocal.

What if the segment is horizontal?

Its perpendicular is vertical. A vertical line is described by its fixed x-coordinate.
mistakes: Use the midpoint rather than either endpoint in the new line equation.
Changing the sign alone does not normally give the gradient at a right angle.
Do not divide by zero to find a perpendicular to a horizontal line.

examples.title: Locate the midpoint of the given segment
examples.question: Find the midpoint of the segment joining \(A(1,-5)\) and \(B(9,5)\).
examples.solution:
Find the mean of the two horizontal coordinates, and then of the two vertical coordinates.

The two averages are \(5\) and \(0\).

The coordinates are \((5,0)\).

examples.title: Use a midpoint and negative reciprocal together
examples.question: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \(A(1,-7)\) and \(B(11,5)\).
examples.solution:
The midpoint is \((6,-1)\). The segment gradient is \(\frac{6}{5}\), so the bisector has gradient \(-\frac{5}{6}\).

The point-gradient equation is \(y-(-1)=-\frac{5}{6}(x-6)\). Expand or rearrange to an equivalent line equation.

The equation is \(y=-\frac{5}{6}x+4\).

examples.title: Find the perpendicular bisector of a horizontal segment
examples.question: Find the equation of the perpendicular bisector of the segment joining \(A(1,-2)\) and \(B(13,-2)\).
examples.solution:
The segment is horizontal, so its bisector must be vertical. Its midpoint is \((7,-2)\).

Every point on this vertical line has x-coordinate \(7\).

The equation is \(x=7\).

The bisector must pass through the midpoint and meet the segment at a right angle.

marking_criteria.description_html: The segment is horizontal, so its bisector must be vertical. Its midpoint is \((212,3)\).
The midpoint is \((224,-2)\). The segment gradient is \(\frac{4}{7}\), so the bisector has gradient \(-\frac{7}{4}\).
